title: Teacher pay: everything you need to know about the latest multi- year pay award

content.content: Here’s everything you need to know about teacher pay.

The School Teachers' Review Body (STRB) is an independent group that makes recommendations on the pay of teachers and leaders in maintained schools in England and reports to the Secretary of State for Education and the Prime Minister.

Each year the STRB recommends a pay award based on different factors including the economy, school workforce data and evidence from organisations including the DfE, employers, and unions.https://educationhub.blog.gov.uk/category/trade-unions/
The government then considers the recommendations in depth and makes a decision on what pay award teachers receive.
In order to give schools and teachers more certainty over pay and their budgets, the Education Secretary asked the STRB’s to make recommendations for a multi-year pay award for the next two years.
Are teachers getting a pay rise?

The STRB recommended that from September 2026, teachers and leaders will receive a pay award of 3.5%, followed by a further 3% increase from September 2027. These recommendations have been accepted in full, reflecting the crucial role teachers play in breaking the link between background and success for pupils.

This means school teachers will see an increase in their pay of 17% since this government took power - equating to almost £7,900 over four years - with the average school teacher salary rising to over £52,800 from September 2026 and over £54,400 from September 2027.
You can calculate how your salary could change following pay award here.
Will teachers at all schools receive the pay award?
The pay award applies to maintained schools currently, but most academies also choose to follow the statutory pay arrangements in practice.

Through the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act, the government will ensure all teachers in academies as well as maintained schools can rely on a core pay offer and will require academies to have regard to the School Teachers Pay and Conditions Document, expected to be implemented by September 2027.
We will continue to increase flexibilities into the national pay and conditions framework so that all schools can innovate to attract and retain brilliant teachers.
Is the pay award fully funded?

This multi-year pay deal award is backed by a significant additional investment of £700 million in 2026-27 and £1.1 billion in 27-28, meaning a total of £1.8 billion more for schools over the next two years, on top of the funding increases which the government has already provided through the 2025 Spending Review.

Recent valuations to the Local Government Pension Scheme will see a 4.9ppt reduction in employer contribution rates and deliver significant savings on schools’ pay bill for support staff. We can confirm this reduction in costs will not be clawed back and as such, we are confident that schools will be able to cover the costs of the teacher pay award, at a national level.
As with the rest of the public sector, schools will continue to maximise value from their budgets.
How can schools maximise and get better value from their budgets?
We know this is not an easy task. Schools are already working hard to manage pressures on budgets.  That’s why we are providing support through the Maximising Value for Pupils programme.

Through the programme we are using the collective weight of the entire school system to help every school get more from every pound, so that money reaches the classroom where it matters most. This includes help to cut the cost on things like energy and recruitment, as well as providing better banking solutions.
For example:
When will teachers receive their pay rise?

The pay award now goes through a 12 week period of consultation with unions and employers’ organisations. The school teachers' pay conditions (STPCD) which sets out teachers pay and conditions, will then be published in mid-October for schools to implement. The pay award will be back-dated to 1st September.
Will school support staff get a pay rise?

The teacher pay award only applies to school teachers, but the additional funding schools will receive also takes into account the current pay offer for support staff, which is currently under negotiation.

Unlike teachers, most school support staff are currently employed on the pay and conditions of the National Joint Council (NJC) for Local Government Services. The NJC is a negotiating body made up of representatives from trade unions and local government employers.  NJC employees have been offered a 3.3% pay increase from 1 April 2026, which remains subject to agreement through the NJC collective bargaining process.

The School Support Staff Negotiating Body (SSSNB) is expected to be established from this autumn to give support staff like teaching assistants, caretakers and cleaners a stronger voice. The body will bring together employer and employee representatives to negotiate pay, terms and conditions, and to advise on training and career progression.
Will further education teachers get a pay rise?

The Department for Education does not set further education pay. However, we are providing £485 million in additional funding over two years to support colleges and other further education providers to address immediate staffing pressures, boosting opportunity for learners and driving skills for growth.
What else are you doing to ensure teaching is an attractive profession?
We are continuing to work alongside schools and colleges to re-establish teaching as the attractive, expert profession it should be.

This includes investing hundreds of millions of pounds to offer tax free financial incentives and professional development to attract and keep brilliant teachers alongside targeted action to improve teachers’ wellbeing.

This is working with the latest figures showing the government is on track to meet its manifesto pledge to recruit and retain an additional 6,500 expert teachers with 4,654 more secondary school, special school and college teachers.

We have made strong progress on teacher recruitment and retention with one of the lowest rates of schoolteachers leaving in the history of the school workforce census – at 2,100 fewer teachers than last year, and there has been a 13% rise in people training to teach, with the STEM recruitment target surpassed for the first time since it was introduced.
How are you improving working conditions for school teachers?

We are also making changes to the School Teachers' Pay and Conditions Document. This includes enabling maintained schools to offer modest non-consolidated recognition payments to staff, as academies already do, so they too can offer recognition schemes to reward their staff; increasing flexibility on INSET days so that schools can structure training in the way which works best for staff and pupils, and clarifying the protections for leaders' working time, including the right to uninterrupted breaks and expectations that weekends and, public holiday should ordinarily be preserved as non-working time.

title: Protecting the Thames Basin Heaths: evidence from 15 years of the SAMM Project

content.content: By Zoe Shorter, Project Manager for the SAMM Team, Thames Solent Area Team

This blog explains the findings of an independent evaluation of the 15-year Thames Basin Heaths SAMM Project. Evidence suggests the project is successfully mitigating recreational pressure on protected heathlands, with stable or increasing bird populations despite housing growth, and the report has identified wardening, education and partnership work as key strengths.
Spanning across Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire, the Thames Basin Heaths is a stunning collection of lowland heathland of international importance.

The landscape is home to an incredible range of flora and fauna, including every species of native reptile, rare Silver-studded Blue and Grayling butterflies, a dazzling array of dragonflies, and rare birds including the Nightjar, Dartford Warbler and Woodlark.

For the last 15 years, the Thames Basin Heaths Strategic Access Management and Monitoring (SAMM) Project has worked to reduce recreational pressure on internationally important heathland habitats while helping local communities continue to enjoy them.
This September, we are pleased to share the findings of an independent evaluation of the project.
Building better places for people and nature

The Thames Basin Heaths Partnership brings together local authorities, Natural England, conservation organisations, land managers and other partners to protect the Thames Basin Heaths Special Protection Area, while supporting sustainable development across Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire.

At the heart of the partnership is a simple ambition: that everyone living within Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire, values the Thames Basin Heaths, feels a sense of responsibility towards them and is motivated to help protect them.
As part of this partnership, the SAMM team works towards this through monitoring, education and engagement activities that promote three core messages:
Alongside SAMM, the partnership offer alternative places to walk and enjoy nature, reducing pressure on protected heathlands and helping balance nature conservation with development.

At Natural England, we are committed to building better places where nature and communities can coexist. We believe that nature and development go hand in hand, and that we should harness the power of nature as we face a changing climate.
The work done by the SAMM team directly supports these aims.
Asking the important question: how do we know we’re being effective?
Although reviewing and monitoring were built into the strategic solution from the outset, a formal evaluation of the SAMM Project had never been undertaken.

Discussions with Natural England colleagues and other projects that help reduce the environmental impacts of new development, at the annual National Mitigation Meet Ups, revealed a shared challenge: demonstrating the impact of behaviour change and preventative conservation work.
In 2024, funding was secured to commission an independent evaluation of the SAMM Project, gathering evidence, identifying improvements and helping to inform future delivery of the project.
The review focused on 4 key questions:
Evaluation outcomes
We were delighted to find the evaluation showed the project is delivering on its core aims.

The headline finding though was that despite significant housing growth and increased visitor numbers across the area, protected bird populations have remained stable and in some cases  increased; indicating that the project has successfully mitigated recreational impacts on the Thames Basin Heaths.

The report identifies our wardening, education and partnership work as key strengths of the project. These activities are at the heart of what we do, helping people enjoy the heathlands while understanding how to protect them. Through guided walks, public events, school visits and community outreach, we connect thousands of people with these special places every year.

The evaluation found that wardens are particularly effective at building trust with visitors through regular conversations, while the education programme has grown significantly in recent years. Together, these activities help build awareness, encourage responsible behaviour and inspire people to care for the Thames Basin Heaths.
Turning evidence into action

So far, we've been able to take the findings of this report and begin making some suggested improvements, including expanding our education capacity to meet the demand and making greater use of social media and other digital channels to reach new audiences.
We're also pleased to see the evaluation already generating interest beyond the partnership, with findings being shared and discussed by other teams working in mitigation and nature conservation.
We look forward to 15 more years of fantastic work protecting the Thames Basin Heaths.
Find out more
If you'd like to learn more, we encourage you to:
And if you're visiting your local heathland, please remember our three simple messages: stay on the path, be wildfire aware and help protect these special places for future generations.
You can also make a direct contribution by exploring our volunteering opportunities and getting involved in protecting the Thames Basin Heaths.
Finally, thank you to everyone who contributed to this work, including our partners, Joint Strategic Partnership Board members, Natural England colleagues, stakeholders and the wider SAMM team.
Together, we're building the evidence, partnerships and confidence needed to protect these internationally important heathlands while supporting thriving communities around them.

title: Bluetongue: how the Animal Health and Welfare Pathway can support farmers
categories: Payments to support animal health and welfare

content.content: Bluetongue virus is a notifiable disease that affects sheep, cattle, deer, goats and camelids - alpacas and llamas. It is mainly spread by midges but can also pass through infected semen, embryos or oocytes, or from a mother to her unborn offspring.
This summer’s hot weather has been ideal conditions for midges and helped the virus spread quicker.
Bluetongue cases are increasing across Great Britain. The disease is most prevalent in the Southwest, West Midlands, Northwest of England and in parts of Wales.

All of England is in a bluetongue Restricted Zone. Provided animals are not showing clinical signs, keepers can move animals within England without a specific bluetongue licence or pre-movement testing. Separate restricted zones are in place in Wales and southwest Scotland where there are also bluetongue outbreaks.

With cases rising quickly, testing demand has increased significantly. Defra introduced new reporting measures last week to speed up diagnosis, reduce waiting times and help farmers act sooner to protect their livestock.
In this post, we look at the new measures, steps livestock keepers can take to protect animals and upcoming webinars for more information.
New reporting measures in England for bluetongue
We know this is a difficult time for animal keepers dealing with Bluetongue. Defra and the Animal & Plant Health Agency (APHA) are working with farmers and vets to manage the outbreak.
In England, private vets can now diagnose clear cases of bluetongue after examining affected animals.

The new process makes it quicker and easier to confirm clear cases of bluetongue based on clinical signs. Private vets will contact the APHA to formally confirm diagnosis, instead of taking blood samples for testing.
This means straightforward cases do not need to wait for laboratory results, helping farmers get answers sooner and act quickly to protect their livestock.

The new changes don’t mean a reduction in disease controls. The usual safeguards remain in place. Where a vet cannot rule out suspicion of notifiable disease, including foot and mouth, the usual reporting and laboratory testing arrangements will continue.

These new changes reflect the current outbreak in England, where bluetongue is now widespread and well understood. These measures to help tackle bluetongue sit alongside wider disease surveillance and APHA support.
Details on how to spot and report bluetongue can be found on GOV.UK.
Support and actions for farmers
Sheep and cattle farmers in England can apply for a government-funded vet visit through the Animal Health and Welfare Pathway. The online application takes less than two minutes.
During the visit, vets can check animals for signs of disease, advise on bluetongue risks and suggest ways to reduce them.
Vaccination is the best way to help protect livestock from bluetongue. It is not too late this season, so farmers should speak to their vet and order vaccines as soon as possible.
Government is working with manufacturers to increase vaccine supply. Farmers should start planning for vaccination next year as the virus is likely to overwinter.
Livestock keepers can help reduce the spread of bluetongue by taking a few practical steps:
If you suspect bluetongue or another notifiable disease, contact your vet promptly. You can find more information and guidance on bluetongue on GOV.UK.
Online webinars
The APHA is hosting webinars for vets to help identify bluetongue, share information on testing, and how to report it:

description: In this post, we explain the new bluetongue reporting measures in England, steps livestock keepers can take to protect their animals, and how farmers can access support through the Animal Health and Welfare Pathway.

title: Have Your Say: Shape the Future of Working in Adult Social Care

content.content: Oonagh Smyth CBE is Chief Executive Officer of  Skills for Care, the strategic workforce planning and development body for adult social care in England. Here, she addresses the adult social care workforce on the importance of taking part in the Adult Social Care Workforce Survey.

This is an important time for adult social care. The Prime Minister has been clear about his commitment to supporting the workforce: the government is taking forward the Fair Pay Agreement and looking at the wider changes needed to make social care an attractive and rewarding career, including progression opportunities, training and better support for staff.
People working in adult social care know the job better than anyone. You know what makes it rewarding, what makes it difficult and what would make your working life better.
That is why we want to hear from you.

The Adult Social Care Workforce Survey is an opportunity to share your experiences directly with the Government. The survey is open to anyone who works in a care-related role in adult social care in England. Whether you work in a residential or domiciliary setting – as a care worker, a personal assistant, a manager, or a regulated professional (e.g. nurse, occupational therapist) - your voice matters.
Your experience can help shape what comes next

To make good decisions for tomorrow’s social care workforce, we need strong evidence about the realities of working in the sector today. The survey is your opportunity to help the Department of Health and Social Care understand what is working well, where the pressures are and what needs to improve.
Your voice will inform what the government does next to support the workforce.
Tell us what working in adult social care is really like
There are no right or wrong answers. We want your honest experience, including the positive parts of your work and the challenges you face.
The survey asks about the issues that can affect your day-to-day working life, including:

You may also have heard about Baroness Casey’s Big Conversation on Care. The two exercises complement each other but have different purposes. The Big Conversation invites everyone in England to discuss the bigger questions about the future of adult social care, whereas this survey focuses on the experience of working in care in detail. Each will provide different evidence to inform the future of adult social care.
Why your response matters

The more people who take part, the stronger and more representative the evidence will be. Each response adds to our understanding of working life across adult social care and helps show where change and support are most needed.
Do not assume somebody else will have the same experience or raise the same issues. Your perspective is unique, and without it, part of the picture will be missing.
Your responses will be kept confidential and reported alongside those of other participants. You will not be identified in the survey findings.
Take part in the survey
If you work in adult social care in England, please add your voice:
Take part in the Adult Social Care Workforce Survey – it takes just 20 minutes.
If you are a manager or employer, please encourage everyone in your organisation to participate and support them to complete the survey during working hours.
The future of adult social care should not be shaped without the people who work in it. Make sure your experience is part of the conversation.

description: People working in adult social care know the job better than anyone. That is why we want to hear from you.

title: How we made it easier for millions of users to sign into government services

content.content: This month, the Government Digital Service (GDS) made it faster, easier and more secure to sign into government services.

23 million people are already using GOV.UK One Login to sign in to over 250 UK government services. Now those users can use a passkey to sign in. This will be the same familiar way they unlock their device, for example with their face, fingerprint or passcode. Users will no longer need to remember a password or enter a security code (also known as ‘multi-factor authentication’) to sign in.

Passkeys are recommended by the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) for use wherever possible. They are more secure than passwords and less vulnerable to phishing and other cybersecurity attacks.

In the first month since we rolled out passkeys for GOV.UK One Login, we have already seen 300,000 (almost 10%) of our users are using them. In the years to come, we expect passkeys to save millions a year for the UK taxpayer by cutting the cost of text message-based authentication.
Introducing passkeys is just one of the ways we are making sure that digital public services are simple, trusted, secure and effective.
This is the biggest change we have made to the sign-in experience of GOV.UK One Login since it launched in 2021.
Putting the user first
The principle of designing for everyone is central to our work at GDS. We put this at the heart of our product development process.
To understand user perception and concerns about passkeys, we started by surveying over 2,500 people. We gathered evidence from user research, data analytics and industry insights.

We know that the public are increasingly using biometrics in many parts of their online lives, from banking to online shopping. This change helps create a more familiar sign-in experience and reflects wider changes in how people interact online.

We found that users struggle to remember passwords, so they reuse them and write them down. We also know that entering a security code is hard for many users, especially those with cognitive barriers and low digital confidence, and people who use assistive technology.
Our product strategy at GDS is to focus on meeting the needs of our users. We expect passkeys to cut the time it takes to sign in to GOV.UK One Login by more than half.
Everyone has needs

We know that for GOV.UK One Login users, authentication is not their end goal. It is a step users need to get through to completing a task, such as renewing their driving licence. Signing in should not be an obstacle for users. Passkeys can help remove the need for them to need to think about this step.

We applied this user-led approach to our wider product delivery too. Our design team set out to design our new passkeys user journeys collaboratively, by considering the needs of our technical architects, product managers, software developers, security experts and senior managers. We worked together to build the best possible user experience.

During our design process we ran workshops with developers to ensure design feasibility. They then checked back with designers to ensure usability. We also consulted security, fraud, and privacy experts to meet GOV.UK One Login’s high service quality standards. Our product manager steered our priorities by relentlessly asking "what is the user need?".
Passkeys have been a real collaboration for our team.
User research is a team sport

A design challenge was explaining passkeys in simple terms that our users will understand. This is especially challenging as how users will sign in can be different depending on their device. A passkey could be a fingerprint for one user, or a screen lock PIN for another. If users do not understand what they need to do, this can stop them from setting up a passkey.

Concerns about biometric data privacy can make users hesitate or worry. In reality, the user’s passkey is private. It is securely stored in their password manager. We had to explain technical concepts in clear, accessible language.

So, we tested our journeys with real users, including those with low digital confidence. In the past year we have run three rounds of user research and iterated our designs after each round. We learnt that users did not need to understand how passkeys work to be able to use them with ease. We worked closely with accessibility experts to design and test our journeys to make sure they work for all users, including those who use assistive technology.

We involved our entire product team, including developers, delivery managers, and product managers. They joined planning workshops, took notes during research sessions, and helped to interpret our findings. This helped our team build empathy for our users and gives us confidence that they will understand our service journeys.
Nudging users - learning from the industry

To ease the cognitive burden for users, we reviewed passkeys journeys across all major tech platforms and online services. This helped us to make sure we were giving users familiar, established content patterns.
Using guidelines from authentication industry experts the FIDO Alliance, we prompted users to set up a passkey during relevant moments in their journey, such as when they sign in.

NHS Login had already introduced passkeys. They shared their user-experience design insights with us about what they had learned. We also met with the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to learn from their work and share our designs.
Passkeys are live but we are not finished

To help us test passkeys safely with real users, our developers built a way for us to release our designs gradually to a small percentage of users. This meant we could check for any problems before we rolled them out to everyone.
We will continuously improve our passkeys user experience based on user insights, and by monitoring adoption rates - such as how many users reject passkeys in favour of their familiar sign in method.

It is going to take time for everyone in the UK to adopt passkeys. We know that not all of our users will be ready to use them straight away. But this development is a major step in the right direction for a user experience that is safer, easier and more secure for years to come.

description: Users can now sign in to GOV.UK One Login with a passkey using their face, fingerprint or passcode, without remembering passwords or entering security codes.

title: Building hydrographic capability in St Helena

content.content: Safe navigation relies on accurate hydrographic data, and collecting that data requires skilled surveyors, specialist equipment, and local expertise. For a remote island such as St Helena, located in the South Atlantic, having this capability locally is particularly important.

Through its longstanding partnership with St Helena Government, the UKHO has provided loaned survey equipment and practical training to local teams. This is helping St Helena to collect vital seabed mapping data and support the safe and secure supply of goods to the island community.
Why is supporting hydrographic capacity building important?

Hydrography is the science that measures and describes the physical features of the seabed. Accurate hydrographic data underpins safe navigation, environmental management, and sustainable use of the marine environment. However, collecting and maintaining that data requires specialist equipment, technical expertise, and the ability to undertake surveys on an ongoing basis.

For island nations such as St Helena, developing local hydrographic capability ensures the mariners on board vessels approaching the remote island have access to fit-for-purpose information and helps to maintain the safe and secure supply of essential food and goods for its community.

Hydrographic data also enables coastal states like St Helena to gain further insights into the marine environment. Seabed mapping data provides marine scientists with information on marine habitats, as well as supporting decision-making for environmental protection and management.

As a world leader in hydrography, the UKHO shares its expertise with the global hydrographic community and actively supports the UK Overseas Territories and other partners, to develop their hydrographic capabilities.  In St Helena, the UKHO has provided access to specialist expertise, training, and state-of-the-art hydrographic survey equipment to undertake essential surveys within its port. By empowering local teams to collect, process, and manage hydrographic data themselves, the UKHO supports long-term resilience while improving the information used to update official navigational products.
Building capability through practical training

The capacity development has formed part of a longstanding partnership between the UKHO and St Helena Government, which aims to strengthen local hydrographic capability and support the collection of high-quality seabed mapping data around the island.

Following an introduction to hydrographic surveying and the systems involved, UKHO hydrographic experts spent two weeks working alongside marine stakeholders in St Helena. They shared practical surveying techniques and provided hands-on training in the use of the UKHO’s loaned survey equipment. Staff from St Helena’s Geographical Information Systems, Marine and Meteorological departments developed the skills needed to collect, process and manage seabed mapping data independently.
Using new technology in St Helena

Through its Hydrographic survey Equipment Loan Pool (HELP), the UKHO provided access to an uncrewed surface vessel (USV) equipped with an advanced multibeam echosounder.  The all-in-one survey platform enabled the team to begin surveying the island's waters immediately.  UKHO hydrographic experts then worked alongside local stakeholders, providing hands-on training and building the skills and confidence needed to operate the system safely in shallow and coastal waters around St Helena.

As well as supporting hydrographic surveys, USVs can be used in a range of operational situations, including search and rescue activities and environmental monitoring. This makes them a flexible tool for St Helena's marine community, while producing fewer emissions than traditional survey vessels.

The initial training focused on using the USV to monitor the port environment and support the safe arrival of supply vessels. In the next phase, local teams will use the multibeam system on a local vessel to survey St Helena's coastal waters. Enabling local teams to use and maintain this technology is an important step towards building a sustainable hydrographic capability in St Helena.
Devlin Yon, Head of Geomatic Services, St Helena Government, commented on the importance of this type of international collaboration, noting that:
Kerrie Howard, PCA Programme Manager, UKHO said:
What happens next?

This approach demonstrates the UKHO’s ongoing commitment to support its partners globally to strengthen their hydrographic capabilities. It also signals a change in how we support our partners, focusing on enabling and empowering our partners to develop their data collection capabilities.

The UKHO will continue to work with St Helena and its partners, to ensure the data collected meets international hydrographic standards (IHO S-44) and UKHO’s data requirements for producing trusted products and services. While St Helena was the first beneficiary of equipment from UKHO’s HELP, the pool is currently being expanded to support more UK Overseas Territories and UKHO partner nations. As a global leader, the UKHO is proud to support nations across the globe to provide access to equipment that may not otherwise be accessible and empower local hydrographers to undertake the surveys of their own waters.

Based on feedback from the hydrographic community in developing countries which the UKHO supports by providing charting services, the UKHO anticipates that the HELP will expand further in years to come to meet the demand. By providing our partners the skills and access to the equipment needed, UKHO aims to increase the quantity of modern data supplied by its partners for vital ports and to enable the development of the next generation of S-100 products.

description: Through its partnership with St Helena Government, the UKHO is helping build local hydrographic capability by loaning specialist equipment and providing training and expertise. The programme enables local teams to collect vital seabed mapping data that supports safe navigation and informed management of the marine environment.

title: There is no such thing as a typical Fast Streamer
authors: Olviya Silvary, Fast Stream Data Analyst

content.content: I almost ruled myself out

When I graduated with a degree in English Language and Literature, I had no idea what to do next, and a lot of anxiety around that decision. When I was accepted onto the Digital Fast Stream, I had to think carefully whether it was the right fit for me.
Looking back, I realise I nearly ruled myself out because I had an idea in my head of what a "typical" Fast Streamer looked like. The truth is, there isn't one.

The Fast Stream is a Civil Service development programme that accelerates careers through a series of postings across different government departments. For me, the Digital Fast Stream has not only exposed me to exciting and varied opportunities, but it has also sharpened my focus on my future career. Whoever you are, read on to find out why it could do the same for you, even if you don’t have a technical background.
Jumping into the deep end

I don't usually deal well with change, so knowing I had only 12 months in each posting to assimilate into the team and wider department was incredibly daunting. I'd also never had a classic office job before. I had only worked in retail and community outreach, so I was often on the go. Sitting in an office and meeting my team on a laptop screen was a real change and a real challenge in some ways.

However, my team in the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) is a fantastic, welcoming group of people. I'll be the first to say I am a chronic oversharer. My cheery morning greetings certainly took some people by surprise, but I settled in quickly. The Digital, Data and Technology (DDaT) directorate functions fluidly. It's common for people to move between professions and teams, with an emphasis on Learning and Development.
This aligns well with the purpose of the Fast Stream, which emphasises professional and personal development. The Fast Stream journey is not just about depth of learning, but variety of exposure.
The Digital Fast Stream: who is it for?
Another reason to be daunted by joining the Digital Fast Stream was that I had no data experience coming into the role. Sure, I was keen to learn, but how far would that take me?
This is not uncommon in the Fast Stream. There were many people coming into the graduate scheme from a completely different career, like 2nd year Digital and Cyber Fast Streamer Collette Ovenseri:

The Fast Stream is often thought of as a graduate scheme, but the 2025 recruitment data tells a different story. Last year 35% of successful applicants were over 23, suggesting a significant number of people on the scheme did not join straight from their undergraduate degree.

Girish Joshi, a Data Analyst and another first-year Fast Streamer in my team, previously created hot sauces and worked as a cruise ship chef. He has shown me definitively that the Fast Stream is not just for graduates:

A lot of people do also assume that it is just for people who have never worked in the Civil Service before. The scheme also accepts existing Civil Servants, for whom the degree requirements are waived. Those already working in the Civil Service may be surprised to hear that the Fast Stream still offers new experiences, opportunities and perspectives. Steve Corder, a Senior Product Manager, shares his experience.
You can make a difference as a Fast Streamer

Over the past year, I have not just contributed to my team but integrated into it. I've helped run the Data Challenge and worked on a wide variety of projects with stakeholders across government. Soon I will help welcome the next cohort of Fast Streamers at Base Camp. Andy Palmer, BIST's Senior Capability Manager says:

While it can be intimidating joining a programme like the Fast Stream, remember that the Civil Service benefits from our perspectives, just as much as we benefit from the experience. As Andy says, “we're stronger for the diversity of experiences Fast Streamers bring”.
Looking ahead

The Fast Stream doesn’t just teach digital skills, it builds flexibility and resilience. Fast Stream graduate and Senior Content Designer, Mei Mei Loh explains how that prepares Fast Streamers for future roles:

I'm not quite sure where the future will take me, but right now, I want to be fulfilled. I want a career where I am constantly adapting to new things, to be challenged on what I know and don't know, and to always keep learning. I've never been very good at standing still, and that's something the government doesn’t do either. I don't want to necessarily be the best there is, but someone who is always pushing for better. What better place for that than the Civil Service?
Is the Fast Stream right for you?

As October (and my next placement) approaches, I don't think I will ever be rid of the fear of the unknown. What I have learned from the Fast Stream, however, is that moving between teams and diving into unfamiliar environments gives you opportunities to grow.
If you are:
Then my advice to you is don’t rule yourself out.
Explore the Digital scheme. Applications open in October, and hopefully we'll see you in DDaT next autumn!

description: Read about how the Digital Fast Stream is helping participants build resilience and confidence in their Civil Service careers

title: What the ‘Early Years’ Innovation Challenge showed us about data-sharing and collaboration
authors: Emily Ball, Deputy Director, GDS Local

content.content: What would a future of seamless, trusted data-sharing mean for how we deliver early years support for children and families?

This was the question at the heart of the Early Years Innovation Challenge day in Sheffield on 9 September. It brought together more than 100 people from local and central government, health, education and partner organisations to explore how better data-sharing could support earlier intervention and improve outcomes for children and families. GDS Local delivered the event with No.10 North, the Local Government Association, South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority and the National Data Library.

The event was part of the new Digital Devolution programme announced by the Prime Minister on 21 August. Through the programme, GDS is working closely with Mayoral Strategic Authorities, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and No.10 North to strengthen digital capability, improve access to data and help local leaders deliver better services.

The event was not a traditional consultation. Participants worked together in teams on a clearly defined set of problems, created and tested possible solutions and identified where local action needs support from central government. This encouraged them to creatively solve problems, as they would in a more traditional hackathon.
Why better data-sharing matters

Considerable information about child development already exists across health, education and local services. However, it is often held in different systems and organisations and in different formats with differing rules about who can see what.

Whist security and responsible use of data is important, this can make it hard for professionals to access the information they need to make the right decision at the right time. Families may have to repeat information to different services, while opportunities to provide earlier support can be missed.

The challenge was grounded in the National Data Library’s Early Years Kickstarter. This work is investigating how health and education data could be brought together safely and securely to help children receive the right support earlier, putting the family at the centre of support, rather than the services.
The event allowed participants to build on that work and consider what a more connected future could look like.
One theme became clear: the problem is rarely a lack of data. The greater challenge is enabling organisations to share and use existing information in trusted, effective and child-centred ways.
How an Innovation Challenge works
Innovation Challenges work best when there is a clear outcome to explore from several different perspectives and participants have a genuine opportunity to influence what happens next.
They provide a structured way to:
At the Early Years Innovation Challenge, participants worked in multidisciplinary teams on three questions:

The morning focused on understanding user needs, sharing evidence and exploring the current information landscape. Teams then generated and prioritised ideas before developing one concept in more detail. They used service journeys, prototypes and other practical tools to show how their ideas could work.
Each team had a facilitator, clear instructions and time limits for each stage. Subject matter experts were available to answer questions and test assumptions as ideas developed.

The aim was not to promote technology for its own sake. It was to develop approaches that could improve decisions, strengthen collaboration and help practitioners access the information they need at the right time.
Combining local and national expertise
Ideas became more practical when frontline, policy, delivery, data and technical perspectives came together.

Practitioners tested proposals against behavioural archetypes informed by NDL’s user research. This prompted several teams to narrow or adapt their initial ideas, moving the discussion from what data could be connected to what information would help someone make a better decision.
Local authority participants also highlighted the balance needed between local flexibility and national consistency.

Services and pathways will differ between places because they respond to local circumstances. But councils should not have to solve the same underlying problems repeatedly. Participants identified common challenges around information-sharing, identifiers, governance and coordination between national programmes.
Bringing different organisations together helped distinguish where a reusable national approach might be useful and where local flexibility should remain.
What happens next
The strongest concepts developed during the event will be explored in a follow-up workshop with GDS Local and the National Data Library, supporting the next phase of the Early Years Kickstarter.

The requirements, barriers and unanswered questions raised by participants will also be shared with relevant teams across GDS and government departments. This will help identify where further discovery, standards, policy or data work may be needed.
Participants have also been invited to contribute to further research as the National Data Library’s work develops.

The challenge created opportunities to share examples of successful local practice. Councils are already testing approaches, conducting user research and learning what does and does not work in areas such as data matching and service integration. National collaboration can add value by making that work easier to find, reuse and scale.
Supporting digital devolution
The Early Years Innovation Challenge is an early example of Digital Devolution moving from national ambition to practical action.

Digital Devolution is about more than transferring powers. Local leaders also need the infrastructure, tools and partnerships to understand local needs, make informed decisions and improve public services.

Innovation Challenges are one way to turn local insight into practical action. They can bring ideas and understanding of local needs from local authorities into national programmes earlier to identify where central government and local government can work together to solve common problems once, where appropriate – a key mission of GDS Local.
To hear more about GDS Local’s work and opportunities to get involved, sign up for the GDS Local newsletter.

title: Sharing the current performance of our ADI services and what we're doing about it

content.content: If you're an approved driving instructor (ADI), a trainee, or a driving school, the chances are you've felt the impact of waiting times. Whether it's a Part 2 or Part 3 test that's taken longer to book than it should, or a standards check that hasn't happened at all, I want to start by being straightforward with you – we know we've got work to do to improve our service.

As the director responsible for DVSA's Enforcement Directorate, part of my role involves overseeing ADI and potential driving instructor (PDI) standards. This means making sure the checks that protect the public and the reputation of this industry are working as they should. Over the past few months, we’ve talked to instructors, trainers and representative bodies about this. Now, I want to set out what we're seeing and what we're doing to improve.
The scale of the pressure

In recent years, we’ve seen demand for ADI qualifications grow enormously. Applications have increased by 152% since 2018/19 and they're still rising. At the same time, Part 3 pass rates have fallen from 33.8% in 2023/24 to 27.7% in 2025/26, meaning more people are retaking their tests. Together, this has put pressure on a testing system that doesn’t yet have the resource it needs to meet demand.

It’s also affected standards checks. In 2024/25, most ADIs did not receive a standards check, which isn't enough to give you confidence that standards are being maintained consistently. I know many of you have raised concerns about this and we’re listening.
Boosting testing capacity

Both problems stem from the same underlying cause. Our examiners who conduct Part 2 and Part 3 tests and standards checks are recruited from our wider driving examiner pool, but they require additional training. Although they are not interchangeable with those conducting car driving tests, resourcing pressures affecting learner driving tests and those affecting ADI and PDI testing are closely linked. I recognise that this has meant ADI and PDI testing hasn't always had the resource it needs.

We're taking steps to change this. We’ll be recruiting new ADI examiners and increasing our training capacity for more ADI examiners to deliver Part 2 and Part 3 tests. If you’re interested in making the move to become an examiner, you can sign up for DVSA email alerts to be notified when the roles go live. Alongside this, we're developing alternative recruitment and training routes into ADI examiner roles which will help increase capacity while having less impact on driving examiner resource.
The qualification process
As well as increasing capacity, we want to look at the qualification process itself to make sure the system is working as well as it can for those going through it.

You'll know that once you've passed the theory test (Part 1), you must pass your Part 2 and book your Part 3 within 2 years, or you'll need to start the whole process again. I want to remind you that if you're waiting to take a Part 2 or Part 3 test and there's no suitable date available, you can use our book to hold service and nominate your preferred test date and test centre location.  This helps inform us where there is demand for ADI practical tests, so we can use our examiner resource to meet that demand.

Too many people are reaching their Part 3 test without the communication and teaching skills the role demands, so we're focusing on how we can support PDIs to start practising these skills earlier. We want to work with the driver training industry to support people being better prepared for their Part 2 tests and beyond. This would help ease pressure on the system.

We've also been working with the industry on a campaign to help people prepare for becoming an instructor, with a particular focus on Part 2. We're reviewing the wider qualification journey with the industry too, to find ways to better support candidates and make sure they're ready when their test comes around.

As part of this wider work with the industry, Darren Russell, ADI Registrar, has written about updates to the driver trainer code of practice and our review of the ORDIT scheme which is well worth a read.
Increasing standards checks

Getting the qualification process right matters, but so does maintaining standards. That's why we've been increasing the number of standards checks we carry out. When we select ADIs for a check, we take a varied approach and performance indicators are just one part of the picture, not the only thing we look at.

There's no fixed time for when you might be called for a standards check, so it could happen at any point. When it does, you'll be asked to demonstrate your teaching in line with the national standard for driver and rider training, the same standard you'll already be familiar with from your day-to-day work with pupils.
Being open about our progress

I know that data and transparency matter to this profession and rightly so. You've told us, and continue to tell us, that you want to see regular reporting on how we’re doing. Last month our Chief Executive, Beverley Warmington, published a blog post about her time at DVSA, which sets out the wider context for the changes ahead.

I won't pretend that these changes will fix things immediately. Some of what we're doing will take months to show results and some of the pressure on the system is likely to continue. But I want you to know that we see this issue clearly, we understand the impact it's had on your businesses and your professional standing and we are working to make changes.
We'll continue to update you as these changes progress and I'd welcome your continued feedback on what's working and where you're still seeing problems.

title: The MHCLG AI Gateway: enabling more effective and safer adoption of AI in our digital services

content.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important part of how we design and deliver digital services. To help product and delivery teams across the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) adopt AI more safely and effectively, our Technical Architecture team developed the AI Gateway – a single, shared departmental platform that gives teams a secure, consistent and faster way to access approved AI technologies.
In this blog post, I share what we did, why we did it and what we learnt.
The problem to solve
Product and delivery teams building digital services in MHCLG need to access AI capability without each needing to spend time designing how that AI access is secure and safe.

Without a central route, multiple teams would end up building separate integrations, governance approaches and support models for different AI services. Repeating this across multiple teams would have created duplication, delays and inconsistent standards.
Our team recognised early the need to focus on the wider organisational challenge affecting all digital product and delivery teams rather than a single technical requirement.
The approach

Our aim was to create a capability that could be reused across the organisation, leading to cost savings, reducing time spent by each team on development and providing one well-managed and scalable solution.
It made sense to create a shared AI platform rather than a series of separate solutions for different AI providers.

Working with colleagues across the wider digital team, we led the architectural approach for the Gateway using Microsoft Azure API Management as the core platform. This gave MHCLG a single governed route to approved AI services, rather than leaving each team to design its own connection pattern.
We wanted the Gateway to be deliberately AI provider-agnostic, and to support models from multiple providers through one consistent approach that supports future integration of additional AI models.
The solution

The solution is a reusable platform with shared controls, common onboarding and a consistent support model. It makes secure AI access available much more easily and much earlier in the development lifecycle than was previously possible through direct API access.

The Gateway is designed to support developers, data scientists, applications and services running in Azure and AWS. This allows AI to be embedded directly into departmental services, not simply accessed from individual devices.
At a departmental level, the platform provides visibility of how AI is being used, enables appropriate technical controls from the centre, tracks costs and supports cost optimisation.
A faster route to AI adoption
By using the AI Gateway, projects can benefit from:
This means delivery teams can focus on solving business problems and improving services, rather than managing the underlying AI infrastructure.
Security and governance by design
As AI becomes more widely embedded into digital services, it is important to maintain the right security and governance controls.
The AI Gateway supports this by:
This creates a safer foundation for innovation and reduces the risks of ungoverned AI access.
Improved visibility and cost management
As demand for AI grows, understanding how it is being used becomes increasingly important.
The Gateway gives teams central visibility of:
This helps teams understand demand, manage spend and make sure AI investment delivers value.
Things we learnt that helped us design the AI Gateway
Build a scalable foundation
Many AI projects begin with one tool, one team or one use case. We recognised early that the solution needed to be able to scale well across a large department.

Building the Gateway on Microsoft Azure API Management and shaping it as a shared departmental platform meant the team can fully integrate with MHCLG’s existing technology stack and leverage the investment already made in this technology.
The team created a practical foundational way for MHCLG to adopt AI safely, efficiently and consistently, while still leaving room for the platform to evolve as the technology changes.
Make sure AI is used safely and appropriately
Responsible use was built into the project from the beginning, with a clear goal of ensuring other teams could use AI safely and appropriately through this solution.

We put the solution through the departmental internal AI approval process along with special technical and data protection approvals to ensure it was assessed against internal policies. Additionally, the Gateway went through penetration testing assessment.

The platform uses existing strong authentication and RBAC access control methods alongside integration into existing monitoring, logging and auditability to provide visibility, with tooling that is backed by commercial contracts and cyber security assurance.

The project was supported by governance documentation covering acceptable use, accountability, operational responsibilities and data handling, and links into the department’s wider AI governance approach, including our AI Register and approval process.

We did not treat governance as something that slows innovation down. We showed that AI can be adopted in a way that is ambitious and practical, while maintaining the right levels of security, compliance and public trust.
Collaboration and focus on user needs

Our team did not approach this work in isolation. We helped shape the architectural direction as part of a wider team effort involving colleagues across digital, Cloud, DevOps, security, governance and delivery functions.

From the outset, the Gateway was designed for shared use across all teams, not just one project or technical area. We worked with colleagues to develop reusable patterns, onboarding guidance, governance artefacts, technical documentation, support arrangements and operational processes.
The impact
The biggest impact has been making AI significantly easier, faster and more efficient for colleagues across the department to adopt responsibly.

Teams now have a clearer route to approved AI services, with common controls, onboarding guidance, monitoring and support already in place. This reduces the cost and time required to develop digital services.

The Gateway has already been adopted by multiple teams and provides access to approximately 20 AI models through a single, governed platform. Several initiatives across MHCLG are already using the platform, with more projects progressing through onboarding.

As a result, colleagues spend less time recreating technical foundations and more time exploring how AI can improve services, support users and deliver better outcomes for the public. The platform provides a strong foundation for wider AI adoption across MHCLG as demand continues to grow.
What’s next
We continue to develop the solution to deliver lasting value to the department, based on providing consistent approaches to governance, security and support.

Our wider roadmap looks to expand the AI capabilities available through the Gateway. Future phases of work will include access to AI services hosted by additional Cloud services providers, giving teams more flexibility while maintaining the same governance, security and operational standards.
If you’re working on similar challenges across government and would like to learn more about this project, get in touch by emailing technology.team@communities.gov.uk.

title: Understand the value of your manure with the Nutrient Management Planning Tool

content.content: Managing nutrients is one of the most important jobs on a farm. If done effectively, it can reduce input costs, maximise crop performance and reduce the impact of farming on the environment.
It can be difficult to know how much nitrogen, phosphate and potash is being applied through manures and other organic materials.

The Nutrient Management Planning Tool (NMPT-GB) is a free online tool, produced by Defra, that helps farmers evaluate, plan and manage nutrients as per crop and soil needs. This helps farmers reduce costs and keep records that support compliance with environmental regulations.
A new update to NMPT-GB makes it easier for farmers and advisers to understand the nutrient and financial value of organic manures to support decision-making.
The update

The NMPT-GB tool now includes an accessible and user-friendly organic manure nutrient calculator which replaces the now outdated MANNER-NPK (Manure Nitrogen Evaluation Routine - Nitrogen, Phosphate, and Potash) tool.
You can access the new update on the NMPT-GB webpage.
MANNER-NPK was a Defra-funded software tool that estimated plant-available nutrients and financial value from organic manures like slurry or farmyard manure.
Historically, MANNER-NPK was available as a standalone download, or accessed through PLANET / Planet4Farmers.
Its calculations are now integrated into NMPT-GB, enabling users to quickly estimate the crop-available nutrients supplied by organic material, and their financial value.
Like the rest of the tool, the new functionality is free to use and can be accessed without completing a full nutrient management plan - as is required for the full NMPT-GB.

At a time where artificial fertiliser prices remain high, the tool supports farmers to reduce reliance on artificial fertilisers and plan nutrient use to be more resilient to global shocks to the fertiliser market.
Testing of the tool over several months helped to shape how it works in practice. Feedback from farmers during testing was positive. A sheep farmer using the tool said:
The financial values were highlighted by other participants, with one arable farmer commenting:

Only farmers and their appointed users will have access to personal and farm data from the tool. Regulators don’t have any access to farm-specific data and will not be able to use the information in the tool to monitor compliance.
NMPT-GB is now live for England and Wales on GOV.UK, with a Scotland release planned for later this year. The MANNER-NPK standalone feature is already available across the three nations.
Defra developed this update alongside ADAS and RSK Business Solutions Ltd with the support of the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB).
Watch our webinar
For more information about the tool and how it can help your farming business, watch our recent webinar:
Get involved
Farmers and advisers tested the tool on real farms over several months, sharing feedback to make sure it works well in practice.
We want to keep improving and developing the tool. Your feedback helps us do that.
Please share your thoughts. You can:

If you’d be happy to keep sharing feedback as the Nutrient Management Planning Tool develops, the best way is to join the Defra Farming Panel. This is completely optional, but it helps us make sure we’re testing improvements with the right people.
You can register your interest by emailing the panel manager, Sophie Werkshagen, at sophie.werkshagen@defra.gov.uk

description: Defra’s Nutrient Management Planning Tool is designed to help make nutrient planning simpler. The online tool has been updated to include a calculator that estimates the nutrients supplied by organic materials and their financial value.

title: Sentinel-3C and FLEX launch into orbit

content.content: From forecasting ocean conditions to understanding how crops respond to drought, two European satellites with key UK contributions have launched together and will expand our view of the Earth in unprecedented ways.

At 2:21 am UK time on 15 September, Sentinel 3C and FLEX launched aboard a Vega-C rocket from the European Spaceport in French Guiana. Sentinel-3C is the latest satellite in the Europe’s Copernicus programme, whilst FLEX is the European Space Agency’s eight Earth Explorer science mission.

Copernicus is the world’s leading Earth observation system, with six families of Sentinel missions that monitor the Earth providing vast amounts of free and openly accessible data that can be used for wide-ranging applications across climate resilience, food and water security, pollution monitoring and civil security.

Sentinel-3C is a mission that observes sea and land surface temperature, ocean and land colour and sea surface topography, which together build a picture of how the Earth’s systems are changing. The Sentinel-3 family of satellites enables various applications including ocean and weather forecasting, wildfire detection and water quality monitoring. For example, Sentinel-3 monitors changes in the colour of the ocean surface to detect and track algal blooms, which can contaminate seafood and degrade coastal air and water quality.

Through ocean forecasting, scientists can monitor their evolution and strengthen their understanding of how the ocean changes in response to the effects of climate change. This allows authorities to assess the potential impacts on marine ecosystems and empowers societies with tools to support the sustainable management of coastal waters and improve water quality.

Sentinel-3 data is also used to respond to ongoing environmental challenges felt here at home. During the European heatwaves this year, Sentinel-3 observations provided valuable insights into land surface temperature, helping authorities assess the impact of heatwaves on communities.

Sentinel-3C also has wider synergies as an integrated element of the European Earth observation system. ESA’s FLEX (FLuorescence EXplorer) mission, which launched on the same rocket and will orbit in tandem with Sentinel-3C, is designed to help scientists understand vegetation health by detecting the faint light plants emit as they photosynthesise. This signal offers a direct window into how efficiently plants are converting sunlight into energy, and how they respond to stress from heat, drought, disease or other environmental pressures.

Together with Sentinel-3C, they form a unique tandem mission where FLEX directly measures plant photosynthesis and Sentinel-3 provides atmospheric, thermal and land-surface context to interpret these signals. Jointly, Sentinel-3C and FLEX deliver an unprecedented capability to provide a more complete view of global vegetation function and status.

The UK is contributing significantly to the success of both missions. On FLEX, TAS UK completed assembly, integration and testing activities on the satellite platform in Belfast, with Teledyne e2v supplying detector hardware for the FLORIS instrument, ABSL supplying spacecraft batteries, Nammo Westcott providing propulsion hardware and the National Satellite Test Facility in Harwell, Oxfordshire, providing large-scale test facilities that subjected the satellite to space-simulated conditions.
Director of the UK Space Agency, Rebecca Evernden said:

On Sentinel-3C, UK scientists and engineers at STFC RAL Space and Airbus Defence & Space played a key role in the design and development of the Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR) instrument, drawing on the UK’s instrument expertise developed through earlier European missions. Teledyne e2v were again involved in detector development whilst ABSL supplied batteries and calibration targets.

Sentinel-3C joins its siblings 3A (launched in 2016) and 3B (launched in 2018), with plans for Sentinel-3C to eventually replace 3A, and be joined by 3D in 2028 to provide data continuity into the mid-2030s. This continuity is crucial because environmental trends are best understood through consistent, long-term records. The European Space Agency have already begun the development of the Sentinel-3 Next Generation missions, which will extend this heritage into the late 2030s.

As Sentinel-3C and FLEX begin their missions, they will carry with them decades of UK expertise, a shared European commitment to understanding our changing planet, and will ensure that Europe continues to have a reliable and independent view of the Earth for years to come.

title: Get ready to meet the new School Food Standards
authors: Finn Morgan, Department for Education Commercial Lead for School Food

content.content: The Department for Education (DfE) has announced a major update to the School Food Standards . This is the first change to the standards since their introduction more than a decade ago.

These standards cover food across the school day including breakfast, breaks and lunchtime. They will become mandatory for all schools in England from the start of the next school year in September 2027.

You don’t have to wait until then though. If your food supply or catering services contracts are up for renewal before September 2027 you should review your options with a view to incorporating the new standards.
The good news is you don’t have to do this alone. We have plenty of guidance and support to help you through the process.
Get help buying for schools
Get help buying for schools (GHBS) is the DfE’s procurement-support service for schools.
The service offers a choice of approved frameworks for the procurement of food supplies and catering services alongside expert advice to guide you through the buying process.
Bespoke support for your school is available from the start to the end of the procurement process, entirely free of charge and delivered by expert DfE procurement staff. They can:
Accessing the service couldn’t be easier. Simply fill in a short form to get in touch.
DfE-approved food and catering buying routes
Our approved frameworks offer both traditional outsourced catering services and food-only options if your school or trust wishes to staff and manage its catering service in house.

Many of the frameworks are provided by public sector buying organisations (PSBOs) run by groups of local authorities. They offer frameworks that cover everything you need - from caterers who can supply your full food service through to kitchen equipment and vending machines.

Also included is the Government Commercial Agency’s own Buying Better Food and Drink framework. This unique framework is especially useful for schools who are considering bringing their provision in house, offering a supply-chain manager who will help you buy the food you need reliably and at a competitive price.
All our frameworks offer significant advantages including:
What you can do now

To find out more about the frameworks, how they can help your school and how you can access them, please sign up to our Food and Catering Buying Solutions Power Hour, which will be delivered online on 13 October . This will be recorded and a link shared with those who register after the session.
In the meantime, you can take these other simple steps to make sure you are prepared for the new School Food Standards  becoming mandatory in September 2027:

title: New school food standards: what parents need to know

content.content: Eating well at school plays an important role in children’s health, wellbeing and ability to learn. That’s why the government has updated the School Food Standards for the first time in over a decade, with a focus on making meals healthier, more balanced and more consistent across all schools.

These changes are designed to ensure every child has access to tasty, nutritious food during the school day, while also responding to concerns from parents about sugar, processed foods and lack of information about school meals.
They come as 500,000 more children are now able to get free meals at school – thanks to the historic expansion of free school meals to children from families on Universal Credit this September.

What are the new School Food Standards?The updated School Food Standards set out clearer rules about the food and drink that schools can provide. They focus on improving the nutritional quality of meals by increasing the amount of fruit, vegetables and fibre, and reducing foods that are high in fat, salt and sugar.
They will apply to all food served in both primary and secondary schools, including both breakfast and lunch.

Why are the changes being made now?Children’s eating habits have changed over time, and many families are concerned about the amount of sugar and processed food in diets. There are also growing health concerns, including rising levels of childhood obesity and tooth decay.
Parents have said they want better-quality food and more transparency. Updating the standards is about making sure school meals reflect modern guidance on healthy eating and meet those expectations.

What will change on school menus?In practice, school menus will shift towards fresher, healthier options. Children can expect to see more fruit and vegetables included in meals, as well as a wider range of balanced dishes.

Foods high in fat, salt and sugar will be limited. Deep-fried foods will no longer be served, and high fat items like pizza or sausage rolls won’t be available every day. Low-sugar desserts are still allowed, such as an apple crumble, raspberry rice pudding or banana bread, but, for most of the week, fruit will be the dessert on offer, along with yoghurt or custard.
The aim is not to take away choice, but to make the healthier option the default.
Will children still enjoy school meals?Schools will continue to offer meals that children recognise and enjoy, but with healthier ingredients and cooking methods.

Menus are expected to include a mix of familiar favourites and new options, showing that nutritious food can still be varied, filling and appealing. Many schools already do this well, and the new standards aim to make that consistent everywhere.
For example, items like spaghetti Bolognese, Mexican style burritos, cottage pie with root-veg mash, jerk chicken with rice and peas and roasted chickpea or a vegetable and mozzarella wrap.

Do the standards apply to breakfast clubs as well?The new standards will cover all food served at school, including breakfast. This means children attending breakfast clubs will also be offered healthier options to help them start the day ready to learn.
This supports the wider rollout of free breakfast clubs in schools, with over 300,000 children now able to access a free club.
How will schools be held accountable?
To give parents greater confidence in school meals, schools will be expected to publish their food policies and menus online, as well as nominate a school food governor.

And to help schools implement the new standards, the government will provide training, resources and guidance. The Department for Education will also work with the Food Standards Agency on an approach to monitoring school food, with more details in the coming months.
When will the changes take place?Some schools may begin making changes straight away, but they will not be in force until September 2027.
There will be a few phased changes on specific foods for secondaries – such as cheese, pulses and drinks – to give schools enough time to make them a success.

How do these changes support families?The updated standards are part of wider efforts to improve children’s health. This includes the expansion of free school meals to more than half a million children from this September and the continued rollout of free breakfast clubs.
Together, these changes aim to make school food healthier, more consistent and easier for families to understand, while helping children build positive eating habits for the future.

title: From curious to confident: how one school transformed its procurement capability

content.content: Professional curiosity about procurement has been transformed into applicable knowledge and skills for Briarwood School finance and business development assistant Sannah Mundy - thanks to the Department for Education (DfE) and the Chartered Institute of Procurement and Supply (CIPS).
Sannah had already been asking about the school’s buying activity when an email arrived in her manager Jacqui Jackson’s inbox offering DfE funded access to the CIPS Digital Academy for a year.

The DfE supports a wide range of training and resources to boost the knowledge and skills of school business professionals. Find out more on our school business professionals: training and development webpage.
The pair quickly agreed this was an ideal development opportunity for Sannah and now; after completing all the modules, she can play a much bigger role in Briarwood’s procurement.
A comprehensive introduction to procurement

The CIPS Digital Academy provides online learning resources covering the full breadth of procurement practice. Accessed via a year-long membership, the platform offers structured modules, downloadable templates, videos, podcasts, think piece articles and links to wider resources.

Users undertake a training needs assessment exercise when first accessing the platform and based on their score, are directed to the most appropriate content at the right level for their existing knowledge.
“It just covered everything from people and leadership to contract negotiation to the supply chains. It was great. It was a whole overview of procurement,” Sannah said.

Sannah's access to the platform was funded by the DfE as part of its support for school business professionals and ongoing commitment to develop commercial and business capability within schools under the Maximising Value for Pupils programme.
Though not specifically focused on education, Sannah found the learning relevant and engaging.

“I've done training before online, but I didn't know what to expect, if I'm being honest,” she said. “I thought it was going to be somebody just talking at me on the screen, but it wasn't, it was so much more than that. It was really interactive.
“Actually, they made it quite fun. Once you finished a module, you would have quizzes and crosswords to do. Overall, it was a really positive experience, and it's definitely helped me with my role.”
Briarwood School is a large and vibrant special school operating across five sites in Bristol, catering for children from infant age through to sixth form, as well as a specialist provision setting.
Better planning and improved efficiency

With around 180 contracts to manage across its sites an efficient operations and finance team is essential to keep things running smoothly. Procurement is a significant and complex part of that which had previously been largely handled by finance and business development manager Jacqui.
Being able to call upon Sannah’s support following her CIPS learning has been a huge benefit to the small but dedicated team with real benefits for the school.
“The school is growing, so we've got quite a lot of procurement coming up and it's wonderful for me to have an extra pair of hands because it can be very time consuming,” said Jacqui.
“We can just work more efficiently now. We're much more likely to get a procurement method right first time and something that's fit for purpose.

“I've only got so many hours in the day, and Sannah can assess something that's needed now and think, ‘OK, three quotes and we'll be fine for that’ or ‘No, we really need a framework, and I've spotted these three that might work’.

“And we can now work a little bit further ahead maybe than we could have done six months ago. In the past it's been a case of us probably already being past a point of need before we could get a procurement going.

“Now we can be a little bit more careful in our planning because we've got that extra capacity and I know Sannah can just start getting on with things for us and that she has very up to date knowledge.”
Building confidence and capability
Sannah too feels much more able to contribute to buying activity since undertaking the CIPS learning.

“Before doing this, my role was finance and business development. I was chasing our debt, putting through invoicing, ordering for the sites, etc. and I knew procurement was happening in the background.

“Now I feel I have a better understanding of exactly what’s involved. When Jacqui is procuring something and asks me to help, I get it. I'm not going back to her with 100 questions. I'm understanding it a lot better.

“Now, I would say, I'd be quite comfortable if she was to give me something to procure. I can say, ‘OK, I know how to go about this’. And if I don't, I can use the templates I got from the modules, mapping the processes, and see exactly what I should be doing.
“It's definitely made me a lot more confident.”

“I think the Digital Academy has definitely built Sannah’s confidence,” agrees Jacqui. “Procurement can be quite a wide-ranging topic and, although she had touched on some admin aspects of it, I think as a concept it just felt quite distant previously.

“But now I think she's got a really good understanding of how procurement works best for us as a school, what the potential is, what the different options are for us, and she's much more confident at dealing with anything and everything to do with procurement.”
